intro: Compare how a design changes with the way a material is worked. A woven panel holds a repeat differently from an embroidered edge, a ceramic relief or painted clay.
alt: Four Andean art studies in a museum showing two textiles, a portrait vessel and a painted bowl.

variants.name: Paracas textile
variants.look: Small, repeated color figures run along the embroidered edge of a darker cloth.
variants.history: Paracas makers on Peru's south coast produced textiles including embroidered mantles. Burial conditions helped preserve many surviving textiles.
variants.when: Look for details where embroidery changes against the weave underneath.
variants.why: Stitches create small independent shapes that can be varied one by one within a repeating border.

variants.name: Inca textile
variants.look: Small squares of intricate pattern create a larger checkerboard across the fabric.
variants.history: Inca authorities gave finely woven garments social and political significance. Rectangular designs known as tocapu appear on surviving textiles.
variants.when: Study how skill and a regular pattern make a garment readable from a distance.
variants.why: The repeated squares unite many detailed units without making the textile feel visually uniform.

variants.name: Moche ceramic
variants.look: A modeled face fills the vessel while the loop and tube of the stirrup spout remain visible above it.
variants.history: Moche potters of Peru's north coast produced stirrup-spout vessels and sometimes used molds to make multiple vessels with the same modeled portrait.
variants.when: Study how a pot can carry a recognizable face and still retain the structure of a vessel.
variants.why: The volume gives the cheeks, eyes and profile dimensional expression as the vessel turns.

variants.name: Nazca ceramic
variants.look: Strong dark outlines separate warm orange, cream and violet designs around the bowl.
variants.history: Nasca artists in southern Peru used varied slips to paint ceramics. Much surviving pottery combines natural forms with complex imagery, including figures whose meanings remain subjects of study.
variants.when: Look for the relation between the painted band's rhythm and the increasing curve of a bowl.
variants.why: The rounded surface keeps some motifs out of sight until the viewer turns the vessel.

prompt: Educational art style comparison board. Exactly four square panels arranged as a 2×2 grid in stated reading order, hairline neutral dividers. Recurring original character is an adult woman with ash-blonde hair in a neat low bun, four-color square hair clip, black rectangular glasses worn throughout, black blazer over knee-length black sheath dress, blue lanyard, blank badge, white coffee mug with four colored squares. She is a visiting museumgoer, visibly present in a corner of each frame. Artwork gets most of the visual space. Scene list in exact order: Paracas textile detail, warmly colored embroidered border against a dark woven field, repeating small figures; Inca textile display of a fragment of tightly woven checkerboard tocapu blocks in reds and ochre; Moche ceramic modeled portrait vessel with a clearly visible stirrup spout; Nazca polychrome ceramic bowl with strong black-bordered orange, cream and violet painted forms against a burnished slip. No lettering, captions, watermark or ornamental frame.
